title: Foam on the river
hook: form like foam, feeling like bubbles, perception a mirage, formations a hollow stalk, consciousness a magic show (SN 22.95)

segments.voice: Yesterday: the arrow, read whole, and your line, one arrow lands, not two. Today the Buddha sits by the Ganges and points at the water.

The Buddha is staying at Ayojjha, on the bank of the Ganges. The river is carrying a big lump of foam downstream. He tells the monks: suppose someone with good eyes looked closely at that foam, examined it carefully. What would they find? Empty, hollow, nothing solid inside. Then, one after another, he names four more things a person might see in an ordinary year. Five pictures.
screen: `ON THE BANK OF THE GANGES.` → `A LUMP OF FOAM, FLOATING BY.` → `LOOK CLOSELY: WHAT'S INSIDE?`

segments.voice: SN 22.95 matches each of the five heaps, the parts of a person from Vajira's chariot, to something you can see. Form, the body, is like that lump of foam. Feeling is like a bubble: in autumn, when it rains in big drops, a bubble rises on the water and bursts. Pleasant, painful, neither: up and gone. Perception, the mind's labeling, is like a mirage in the last month of the hot season, shimmering on the road, convincing, not there. Formations, our habits and intentions, are like a banana tree. A man goes looking for heartwood with a sharp axe. He cuts down a big, straight, young plantain trunk and peels it, layer after layer, and finds no heartwood at all. Not even softwood. And consciousness is like a magic show, a trick put on by a conjurer at a crossroads. Someone with good eyes sees through it. Each picture is chosen carefully. Foam has a shape, but you can't build with it. Bubbles last a moment. A mirage really does look like water. The plantain is layers all the way down. And the magic show doesn't say consciousness isn't happening; it says it isn't what it appears to be. The point isn't gloom. One who sees this way, the Buddha says, grows disenchanted, and through dispassion is freed. The closing verse adds a plain reminder: this body, when life, heat and consciousness leave it, lies cast aside, food for others. Foam is still beautiful on a river. You just don't try to hold it.
screen: `FORM: A LUMP OF FOAM` · `FEELING: A RAINDROP BUBBLE` · `PERCEPTION: A MIRAGE, FORMATIONS: A PLANTAIN` · `CONSCIOUSNESS: A MAGIC SHOW` · then, large: `FOAM ON THE RIVER.`

segments.voice: If you can, look at foam or bubbles right now, the top of a fizzy drink, soap in the sink, a puddle in the rain; if not, picture one clearly, and watch a bubble form, sit, and burst. Then turn to your own feelings as they come, small pleasant ones, small unpleasant ones, and see each rise and burst like raindrops on the river. No need to push any away.
Phena. The Pali word for foam, the image for the body in SN 22.95, where feeling is a bubble, perception a mirage, formations a plantain trunk, consciousness a magic show. Today's word.
Your line: up and gone. Five pictures, and nothing solid to grab in any of them. Day six hundred forty-six.

howItsDone: Some Buddhists contemplate the five aggregates through images like these, and teachers in several traditions use the foam, the bubble and the mirage to teach impermanence.

original.note: Pali phena: foam. SN 22.95 is the Phenapindupama Sutta, the simile of the lump of foam.

trapdoor: what you thought: foam on the river is just a pretty image.
what it means: in SN 22.95, five pictures for the five heaps: foam, bubble, mirage, plantain trunk and magic show, none with a solid core.

what a scholar hears: the foam, bubble and mirage images reappear in later Buddhist literature, including the Dhammapada's verse comparing the world to a bubble and a mirage, and the Mahayana's Diamond Sutra.

chat.says: Why did the Buddha compare the body to foam on a river?
options: Look closely and it's hollow, nothing solid inside: a shape, not something to hold.
Because the body just drifts wherever the river of life happens to push it.
Because foam was the first thing he happened to see that day by the Ganges.
chat.meaning: In SN 22.95, someone with good eyes finds the foam empty and hollow. Form, the body, is like that: a real shape, nothing solid to hold.

Ganges.meaning: a great river of north India

Ayojjha.meaning: a town on the Ganges where the Buddha stayed

heartwood.meaning: the hard, solid core inside a tree trunk

plantain.meaning: a banana plant, its trunk made of layers

notes: SN 22.95 paraphrased. Confirm the setting (Ayojjha on the bank of the Ganges), the five similes in order and their details (bubble in autumn when it rains in big drops; mirage in the last month of the hot season; a young plantain trunk cut down by a man seeking heartwood; a magic illusion displayed by a magician or his apprentice at a crossroads), and the closing verse about the body cast aside when life, heat and consciousness depart.
The trapdoor links to Dhammapada 170 (the world as a bubble and a mirage) and to the Diamond Sutra's closing verse; these are later or parallel texts, please confirm the connection is stated fairly.
